empty-net.label: Diagram: a team pulls its goaltender for an extra attacker, leaving its own net empty.
empty-net.door: See a pulled goalie in our replay

see.say: This is not the only reason a goaltender leaves the ice

steps: Losing late, a team sends its goaltender to the bench.
In the goaltender’s place comes an extra attacker: six skaters against five. Nothing is toggled on this site to show it — the goalie is simply no longer drawn.

steps: In each end — four spots, two on either side of the net. An icing comes back to one of these, in the offending team’s own end.
At centre ice — where a period starts, and where play restarts after every goal.
In the neutral zone — four more, just outside each blue line. A play called back out of the zone usually restarts here.

steps: The puck carrier comes up the ice toward the blue line.
A teammate crosses the line before the puck does — that is offside. The puck has to cross the line completely first: touching it is not being in the zone.
Play stops, and the face-off comes back outside the zone.

penalties.label: Diagram: an official signals a delayed penalty while the other team keeps the puck and pulls its goaltender; at the whistle the offending player leaves the ice for the penalty box.
penalties.door: See a penalty called in our replay
steps: An official raises his arm and play carries on — until the offending team touches the puck. The other side keeps possession, and may even pull its goaltender for an extra skater.

When the offending team touches the puck the whistle goes. The offender goes to the penalty box and his team plays a skater short until the penalty is served — and a goal by the other team ends a minor early.

see.say: A goaltender leaves the ice for one other reason — and it is the more familiar one

penalties.note: Most penalties are one of three kinds: restraint — tripping, hooking, holding, interference; stick — slashing, high-sticking, cross-checking; and physical — roughing, boarding, charging. A few are none of those: delay of game, too many men. They are not all the same length either: two minutes for a minor, four for a double minor — two minors served one after the other — five for a major, and a misconduct is ten. A misconduct is the odd one out: the player sits, but his team is not a skater short, because a substitute takes his place on the ice. A game misconduct sends a player off for the rest of the night. Two calls that arrive together and carry the same time are matching, whatever the two infractions were — both players sit, and the sides stay even.

slot.note: The slot is not rare, and that is the point: __SLOT_ATT_IN__ of __SLOT_ATT_N__ located attempts — __SLOT_ATT_PCT__% — are already taken from inside it. So the shading does not mark where the shots are; it marks where they go in. Blocked shots are in neither count, because the coordinate the feed records for one is where the puck was stopped — the blocker’s position, not the shooter’s.
steps: Close in — within 33 feet of the net. This one counts.
And between the face-off dots. The shaded band is exactly that wide, so you can check a mark against it: this one is too far out to the side.
And in front of the goal line. A shot recorded from behind the net is close to the slot, but it is not from the slot.
